The Grey-headed imperial pigeon (Ducula radiata) is a frugivorous columbid endemic to the montane forests of Sulawesi and its satellite islands. Adult females reach an asymptotic body mass of 295 grams [Wwi = 295 grams], a size that places this species among the mid-range Ducula pigeons, similar in bulk to D. lacernulata but notably smaller than the robust Pied Imperial Pigeon (D. bicolor). This body mass reflects a life history shaped by fruit-resource availability at mid-elevations, where figs and laurel fruits constitute the dietary staple. In stark contrast to the adult dimensions, the egg that produces the altricial squab has an initial wet weight of just 19.2 grams [Ww0 = 19.2 grams]. Such a small initial wet weight—barely 6.5 percent of the maternal mass—is typical of altricial pigeons, whose squabs are blind, nearly naked, and entirely dependent on crop milk provisioning from both parents for the first several days of life. The magnitude of postnatal mass accretion required to attain adult size underscores the high nutritional demands placed on the secreting adult crop epithelium during the early nestling period.

Development within the egg proceeds at a pace dictated by embryonic temperature. In captive breeding observations, embryos of Ducula radiata complete incubation in 25 days [ab = 25 days] when the eggs are incubated at a steady 39 °C [T = 39 °C]. This incubation period is somewhat protracted for a pigeon of its body size, aligning more with the longer developmental times seen in fruit pigeons that lay single-egg clutches and invest heavily in each offspring. The 39 °C incubation temperature is maintained through continuous brood-patch contact by both parents, which alternate incubation bouts throughout the day. Compared to the generally smaller-bodied Columba species that incubate at slightly higher temperatures, the Ducula radiata embryo appears adapted to a cooler thermal environment, possibly reflecting the cooler ambient conditions of its montane habitat. The 25-day duration, combined with the single-egg clutch, results in a slow reproductive pace that constrains the annual output, a theme that recurs throughout the life history of this insular frugivore. The completion of incubation marks the transition from the calcareous egg to the vulnerable altricial nestling, initiating the period of most rapid mass gain.

At the active body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], which represents the typical core temperature of a foraging adult, the post-hatching developmental trajectory partitions into distinct phases. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs remarkably early at only 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This rapid wing-feather growth and muscle maturation allows the juvenile to leave the nest platform and begin independent foraging under parental supervision—a critical milestone in the predator-rich forest canopy. Despite this precocial fledging schedule, the onset of gonadal activity is substantially delayed. Sexual maturity, evidenced by the first signs of gametogenesis and gonadal swelling, is reached at approximately 78 days after hatching [tp = approximately 78 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. The protracted interval between fledging and puberty likely reflects the energetic demands of completing somatic growth, particularly the development of the flight apparatus and the attainment of adult body condition before the organism diverts resources toward reproductive competence. In Ducula radiata, this extended subadult phase may also facilitate the juvenile's acquisition of complex foraging skills required to locate and process ephemeral fruit resources across the montane landscape.

Under the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the reproductive output of Ducula radiata is strikingly conservative. Each breeding attempt yields only 1 egg per clutch [N_R_i = 1 egg per clutch], and females produce no more than 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year]. This minimal annual fecundity is a common trait among large fruit-pigeons that inhabit stable, resource-predictable environments where adult survival is high and each offspring receives intensive parental investment. The onset of actual breeding is likewise postponed: first successful reproduction, marked by the laying of a fertile clutch and subsequent chick provisioning, occurs at approximately 2.3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 2.3 years after hatching], a delay that ensures females have attained full body size and accumulated sufficient somatic reserves at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Once reproductive maturity is entered, individuals may continue breeding for many years; the maximum recorded longevity in the wild stands at 14.3 years [am = 14.3 years] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This combination of low annual fecundity, delayed maturity, and extended lifespan exemplifies the slow life-history strategy typical of island frugivores facing relatively low extrinsic mortality from predators but high stochasticity in fruit crop availability.

Respirometric measurements obtained from adult Ducula radiata at a standard body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] reveal a maximum basal metabolic rate of 253 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 253 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, recorded from fed, resting individuals during the inactive phase, is consistent with the allometric expectations for a columbid of roughly 300 grams body mass and underscores the moderate energetic throughput that sustains the pigeon's largely sedentary, fruit-based foraging ecology. Compared to the lower BMRs reported for smaller granivorous columbids, the metabolic rate of D. radiata likely reflects the relatively low-quality diet of figs and other soft fruits, which demand prolonged gut retention and may elevate specific dynamic action. However, given the cool, humid conditions of the Sulawesi highlands, a BMR in this range probably also functions to sustain endothermy without excessive heat dissipation costs. The reliance on a frugivorous diet, which shows marked seasonal fluctuations in lipid content and availability, may impose further metabolic adjustments across the annual cycle, although long-term field metabolic data remain lacking for this elusive canopy-dweller. Future comparisons with other Ducula species across altitudinal gradients would clarify whether this BMR represents an adaptation to montane fruit diets or a phylogenetic constraint.
